title: A force coefficient is a number with a window, a domain and a reference; read all three before the value
summary: Drag and lift coefficients on a cylinder are the standard check of a flow solver. The figures here show how to read a force time series, a steady drag plateau, a resolution study and a blockage comparison, and why each can disagree with a published value for reasons other than the solver being wrong.

media.alt: Two stacked time series against t (units of D over U) from 0 to 80. Top: drag coefficient, a spike at t = 0 off the top of the axis with an annotation, then a slow decay to about 1.7 near t = 20, a growing wiggle from t = 30, and regular oscillation between about 2.2 and 3.0 after t = 40. Bottom: lift coefficient, flat near zero until t = 30, then oscillation growing to an amplitude of about 3.3. The title gives mean drag 2.560, lift amplitude 3.361 and Strouhal number 0.1495.

read_the_figure.question: Has the flow settled into a steady or periodic state, and what are the mean drag, the lift amplitude and the shedding frequency?
read_the_figure.axes: x: time in units of the cylinder diameter divided by the free-stream speed (D over U). Top y: drag coefficient. Bottom y: lift coefficient. Each curve is one run; the two panels share the time axis.
look_at: Find the start-up transient: the annotation points to a spike at t = 0 that runs off the top of the axis. It comes from the impulsive start and is not part of the physics of the wake.
Follow the lift curve: it is nearly zero until t of about 30 and then oscillates with growing amplitude. That growth is the wake instability that starts vortex shedding.
After about t = 40 both curves are periodic. The drag oscillation is much faster than the lift: count the drag peaks between two lift peaks (two).
Measure the lift period between peaks and convert it to a frequency. The title states a Strouhal number; check it against your own count.
Notice that the lift amplitude printed in the title is larger than the mean drag. Check this against the published values for the same Reynolds number and blockage.
The mean drag in the title is an average over a window that the figure does not state. Averaging over the whole run would include the transient.
read_the_figure.proves: A periodic force signal with a stable amplitude over many cycles shows that shedding has been captured and that its frequency can be measured. Matching a published Strouhal number and mean drag would then support the solver; a mismatch calls for the checks in the other figures.
if_wrong: Amplitude still growing at the end: the run has not reached its limit cycle, so mean and amplitude are provisional.
A start-up spike left inside the averaging window: the mean is biased.
Lift amplitude or mean drag far from reference: a different Reynolds number, blockage, definition of the reference area, or a wall-treatment error.
Drag and lift at the same frequency: a sign that one of the two is mislabelled or that the symmetry argument fails (see the steps).
must_check: The averaging window and the number of shedding cycles in it.
The reference area and velocity used in the coefficients (diameter and free-stream speed here).
The blockage ratio and the outflow distance, which change the drag.
Resolution in grid points per diameter and whether the result is converged against it.
The start-up treatment: the spike should be identified and excluded.
as_drawn: Values read by eye, about 5 percent.
Title: mean Cd 2.560, Cl amplitude 3.361, Strouhal number 0.1495. Annotation: start-up spike of Cd about 318, off scale.
Drag decays to about 1.7 near t = 20, then oscillates between about 2.2 and 3.0 after t = 40 with a period of about 3.4.

Lift peaks near t = 41.5, 48.7, 55.5, 62.2, 69.2 and 75.9, with amplitudes of 2.9 to 3.5; the period from 41.5 to 75.9 over five cycles is 6.9, a Strouhal number of about 0.145 (computed), consistent with the title to about 3 percent.

Companion figures: steady drag at Re = 20 and 40 reads 2.553 and 1.955 against literature values of about 2.05 and 1.55 drawn on the plot; the resolution study reads 2.465 and 2.553 at 18.6 and 26.6 points per diameter, with a diverged point at 37.3; the blockage study reads about 2.55 (10 percent, flat) and 2.355 falling to 2.328 (5 percent, still decreasing) between t = 11.5 and 15.

terms.meaning: Force components on the body, made dimensionless with the dynamic pressure and the diameter (force per unit length in 2D).
The ratio of inertial to viscous effects for the flow past a cylinder of diameter D.
The periodic release of alternate-sign vortices from the two sides of a bluff body above a critical Reynolds number.
The body's diameter divided by the width of the domain. Confinement speeds the flow past the body and raises the drag.
The number of grid cells per diameter. It controls how well the boundary layer on the body is represented.
A way to impose a solid body on a regular grid by adding a strong damping force inside the body region. The drag can be computed as the integral of that force.
The artefact of starting the flow impulsively from rest, which gives a very large initial force that decays quickly.

remember: The drag signal oscillates at twice the lift frequency: the two sides shed alternately, and the drag does not care which side.
Averages need a stated window of whole cycles after the transient.
Confinement raises the drag; a smaller blockage ratio lowers it toward the unconfined value.
A grid study needs at least three grids in the asymptotic range; two points give a trend, not an order.
A diverged run is information: show it, mark it, and do not average it in.
Compare with a literature value only at the same Reynolds number, blockage and definition.

understand.title: Four views of one verification question
understand.text: The steady figure asks whether the drag has settled (flat plateau) and how far it sits from published values. The time-series figure asks the same for the unsteady case and adds frequency and amplitude. The resolution figure asks whether refining the grid brings the answer toward the reference. The blockage figure asks whether the domain is large enough. Each can explain part of a gap to the literature, and all four must be read together.

understand.title: The drag is high in every figure
understand.text: At both steady Reynolds numbers the drag lies about a quarter above the literature value drawn on the plot (24 and 26 percent, computed), which looks like a systematic offset rather than a Reynolds-number effect. The blockage figure shows that part of this is confinement: halving the blockage lowers the drag by at least 0.2, and the 5 percent run was still falling. Penalisation thickness and resolution also move the value; the figures do not separate these effects, and the owner may wish to isolate them with one-factor runs.

understand.title: A diverged run is shown as a diagnostic
understand.text: The finest grid in the resolution study diverged at its time step, so its marker is a short run at a smaller time step and is not converged. Showing it is honest, and it should be read as a warning that the stability limit of the time step tightens with resolution, rather than as a data point on a convergence curve.

steps.title: Definition of the coefficients
steps.tex: C_d=\frac{2F_x}{\rho U^{2}D},\qquad C_l=\frac{2F_y}{\rho U^{2}D},\qquad St=\frac{fD}{U},\qquad Re=\frac{UD}{\nu}
steps.note: Force per unit span divided by dynamic pressure times diameter. With time in units of D over U the frequency f in the figure's units is the reciprocal of the period, so St = 1 / T directly.

steps.title: Why drag oscillates at twice the lift frequency
steps.note: Half a shedding period later the wake is the mirror image of itself about the centreline. The lift changes sign under the mirror, the drag does not, so the drag repeats every half period. In the figure the drag period is about 3.4 and the lift period about 6.9.

steps.title: Strouhal number from peak spacing
steps.note: Pick N successive lift peaks. Spacing over many cycles averages out the reading error.

steps.title: Deviation from a reference
steps.note: Relative deviation: for the two steady cases (2.553 against 2.05 and 1.955 against 1.55) it is 24.5 and 26.1 percent. Similar relative deviations at two Reynolds numbers hint at a common cause such as blockage or penalisation, not a Reynolds-number-dependent error.

steps.title: Blockage and the domain
steps.note: The domain heights in the vorticity figure (about 10 diameters tall) correspond to the 10 percent case. The confinement correction is not a constant: it depends on B and on Reynolds number, so it should be measured by a run, not subtracted by formula.

steps.title: Observed order needs three grids
steps.note: With three grids of constant refinement ratio r. In the resolution study there are two valid grids, so no order can be fitted; the trend is that the drag increases with resolution, away from the reference. Two points cannot distinguish an asymptotic approach from a drift.

steps.title: Why a finer grid can need a smaller time step
steps.note: Explicit time stepping has an advective and a diffusive stability limit that both tighten as the grid is refined, and a penalisation term adds its own limit proportional to the penalisation parameter. A run that diverges at fixed dt on a finer grid is the expected behaviour.

worked.title: Strouhal number and drag frequency from the time series
worked.problem: Lift peaks are read at t = 41.5, 48.7, 55.5, 62.2, 69.2 and 75.9. Estimate the Strouhal number and the drag oscillation period.

solution.text: Mean peak spacing over five intervals.
The drag period is half the lift period.

worked.answer: St is about 0.145 (the title says 0.1495, a 3 percent difference that is within the accuracy of reading peaks by eye); the drag oscillates with a period of about 3.4, matching the figure.

analyze.q: The Cl amplitude in the title is larger than the mean Cd. Name two checks that would tell you whether this is a real result or a symptom of the set-up.
analyze.hint: Compare with published amplitude at the same Re and blockage; check the force integral and the definition of the reference area.

analyze.q: The steady drag is about 25 percent above the reference at both Re = 20 and 40. Propose a set of runs that would separate the contributions of blockage, resolution and penalisation parameter.
analyze.hint: Change one factor at a time and keep the rest fixed.

analyze.q: In the blockage study the 5 percent run is still decreasing at the last time. What would you conclude and what would you do next?
analyze.hint: Run longer until the slope is zero within a tolerance.

evaluate.q: Is it acceptable to report the diverged finest-grid value in the resolution plot? Under what conditions?
evaluate.hint: It must be labelled and excluded from any fit.

evaluate.q: What does a match of the Strouhal number alone prove about the solver, and what does it leave open?
evaluate.hint: Frequency is insensitive to some force errors.

create: Redraw the time-series figure with a shaded averaging window of whole cycles, the transient greyed out, and the mean and amplitude printed with their window.
Design a three-grid, two-blockage study table that would allow an observed order and a confinement correction to be quoted with an uncertainty.

checks.q: Why does the drag oscillate at twice the frequency of the lift?
checks.hint: Mirror symmetry of the wake after half a period.
checks.answer: After half a period the wake is the mirror image of itself. Lift changes sign under mirroring but drag does not, so the lift needs a full period to repeat and the drag only half.

checks.q: Lift peaks are separated by 6.7 time units. What is the Strouhal number?
checks.hint: St = 1/T in units of D over U.

checks.q: Drag at Re = 20 is 2.553 against a reference 2.05. What is the relative deviation, and what does a similar deviation at Re = 40 suggest?
checks.hint: Divide the difference by the reference.
checks.answer: (2.553 - 2.05) / 2.05 = 24.5 percent. A similar percentage at the other Reynolds number (26 percent) suggests a common cause, such as blockage or the wall treatment, rather than something that depends on Reynolds number.

checks.q: A colleague fits a convergence order through the two converged points of the resolution study. Comment.
checks.answer: Two points give a slope, not an order with a check: an order needs three grids in the asymptotic range. The trend, with the drag increasing away from the reference, is a warning that something other than discretisation error dominates.

checks.q: How would you set the averaging window for the mean drag in the time series?
checks.answer: Detect when the amplitude of the lift has become constant, discard everything before it, and average over an integer number of lift periods, repeating with one fewer and one more period to see the sensitivity.
